answer: A deposit-backed identity registry resists sybils by making each identity costly: an agent must lock a refundable stake before it can transact, and proven fraud slashes that stake. Like a juniper that only takes root in firm soil, identities grow slowly through earned reputation rather than springing up overnight. At the nadir of trust - a fresh, unproven account - limits are tightest, so a flood of new identities gains nothing. Honest agents eventually reach the calm lagoon of full access, while attackers who burn deposits on fake accounts run dry before they can profit.
